title: The Professional Poker-Face Trap
hook: Many men learn at work to show nothing, and then discover that a face which gives nothing away also invites nobody in.
why:
In many workplaces, a still face is treated as a professional virtue. Traders, lawyers, surgeons, police officers, managers and salesmen learn to keep their reactions to themselves: not to flinch at bad news, not to look pleased too early, not to let a client or a rival see what they think. Composure has real uses. But many men carry it everywhere, into every meeting and conversation, until a face that was meant to protect them starts to cost them.

This chapter is about that cost. It covers where the professional poker face comes from; the evidence that expressive people are trusted more; how other people use your face as information, and what they assume when there is none; the trade-off between warmth and competence in a smile; what happens when the face is wrong for the moment, as in a corporate apology; the toll of acting all day; and how to be selectively expressive, keeping composure for the moments that need it. The chapter on the mask in Part II looked at hiding distress; this one looks at the everyday face of work.

teach.h: Where the poker face comes from.
teach.p:
Few men decide to have a poker face. They learn it. Some learn it at home, from fathers who did not show feelings. Some learn it at school, where showing hurt invited more of it. Many learn it at work, in cultures that equate a still face with strength, control and seniority, and that punish visible doubt, frustration or enthusiasm as unprofessional.

The chapter on reading yourself under stress in Part VI described the psychologist Ronald Levant's argument that many boys are taught to stop noticing and naming soft feelings. The professional poker face is the adult version, applied to the face. Men learn to give no reaction to a colleague's idea until they have decided what they think of it, to stay expressionless when a client pushes back, to receive praise and criticism with the same flat look.

The habit often starts as protection, and it often works. A face that gives nothing away cannot be used against you in a negotiation, cannot reveal panic in a crisis, cannot be accused of favouritism. In certain moments, as the last block of this chapter describes, those are real advantages.

The trouble is that most of working life is not a negotiation or a crisis. It is collaboration: people trying to understand each other, decide whom to trust and work out what is going on. In those settings, a face that shows nothing does not read as strength. It reads as nothing, and people fill the gap with their own guesses. The figure here stands at rest, face neutral. In a mirror, it looks composed. Across a meeting table, for an hour, it can look like disapproval, boredom or contempt.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's inexpressiveness at work were mostly a matter of temperament rather than learning. Temperament plays a part, and some people are naturally less expressive, but the norms of many workplaces clearly reward and teach composure.
teach.pullQuote: A face that shows nothing does not read as strength. It reads as nothing, and people fill the gap with guesses.

teach.p:
In 2003 Thomas Boone and Ross Buck argued that emotional expressivity evolved partly as a signal of cooperativeness. Because spontaneous expressions are hard to fake, they suggested, people who show their feelings give others evidence about their intentions, and others are right to trust them a little more.

Later studies have supported the idea. In 2010 Joanna Schug and her colleagues found that people who behaved cooperatively in economic games were more emotionally expressive than those who did not. In 2007 Eva Krumhuber and her colleagues found that people in a trust game trusted partners who smiled genuinely more than partners who did not, and trusted partners whose smiles looked fake less.

The point is not that every expressive person is trustworthy. Some are skilled at performing feeling, and the chapter on deception in Part I described how poorly anyone detects lies. The point is that a blank face gives other people no evidence at all, so they cannot calibrate their trust. In collaborative work, where people need to decide whom to rely on, that is a disadvantage.

The figure here listens attentively, his face responding to what he hears. Interest, surprise, amusement and concern pass across it as the speaker talks. To the speaker, those small movements are evidence that he is being heard by someone with a mind and a stake in the outcome. A still face, however attentive behind it, offers none of that evidence.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if expressive people were trusted no more than inexpressive ones. Studies of expressivity and cooperation mostly find an association, though the effect depends on whether expressions look genuine, and skilled performers can exploit it.

teach.h: Your face is other people's information.
teach.p:
The psychologist Gerben van Kleef has argued that emotions are a form of social information. People watch each other's faces to work out how things are going and what to do next. A colleague's smile says the idea is landing; a frown says it is not; a look of concern says something is wrong. People adjust their behaviour accordingly, often without noticing.

A manager with a poker face withholds that information from everyone around him. His team cannot tell whether he likes their work, whether a meeting went well, whether he is worried about the quarter or whether they are in trouble. And people do not respond to missing information neutrally. As the chapter on silence described, gaps tend to be filled with the worst available interpretation. A blank face after a presentation is read as disappointment. A blank face in a one-to-one is read as dissatisfaction.

The result is often the opposite of what the poker face was meant to achieve. People stop bringing problems, because they cannot predict the reaction. They over-prepare, second-guess and look elsewhere for signs of how they are doing. Good news is delivered late, and bad news later still.

The figure here sits back with arms folded, face neutral. He may be thinking hard, approving, tired or quietly pleased. Nobody in the room can tell, and so each of them is likely to decide, privately, that he is unimpressed.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people treated an unreadable face as neutral rather than filling the gap with interpretations. Research on emotions as social information and on ambiguity suggests they do not, though how they fill the gap depends on the relationship and the setting.

teach.p:
If showing more is generally better, is a big smile always best? Not quite. In 2017 Ze Wang and his colleagues showed people photographs of marketers and service providers smiling slightly or broadly. Broad smiles made them seem warmer but less competent than slight smiles. The trade-off mattered most when the stakes were high: when people were choosing a service where mistakes would be costly, competence counted for more, and the broad smile cost more.

The researchers also looked at crowdfunding pages and found that creators with broader smiles in their profile photos tended to raise less money, though that analysis was observational.

Other research points the other way. The study of video backgrounds described in the chapter on camera height found that smiling made people seem both more trustworthy and more competent. The difference may lie in intensity: a warm, moderate smile seems to help on both counts, while a very broad, beaming smile in a serious setting may tip toward seeming less competent.

For men who have trained themselves out of smiling at work, the practical message is to turn the dial up from zero, not to beam. A real, moderate smile when greeting someone, when an idea is good or when something is funny adds warmth without costing authority. In high-stakes moments, such as presenting to a board or delivering a diagnosis, a slight smile and a steady face may serve better. The figure here stands open and at ease. Warmth does not need a grin.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if smile intensity made no difference to judgments of warmth and competence. Wang and colleagues found a trade-off, but other studies find that moderate smiles help on both counts, so treat the effect as dependent on intensity and context.

teach.h: When the face is wrong for the moment.
teach.p:
Sometimes the trouble is not too little expression but the wrong one. In 2015 Leanne ten Brinke and Gabrielle Adams studied video of executives making public apologies for corporate failures, coding their facial expressions frame by frame, and compared them with how their companies' share prices moved afterwards. Executives who smiled while apologising tended to see their share prices do worse than expected. Executives who looked genuinely sad tended to see the damage contained.

In a follow-up experiment, people watched an actor playing an airline chief executive apologising for a computer failure that had stranded thousands of passengers. When he looked sad, viewers judged him as more sincere and were more willing to keep doing business with the company than when he smiled or looked neutral.

The finding fits the chapter on apology in Part III: an apology is judged by the body delivering it. A smile during an apology may be meant as warmth or as nerves, but it reads as not taking the harm seriously. A poker face reads much the same way.

The broader lesson is that expression is not a dial to be set once. It must fit the moment. Concern when someone brings bad news, pleasure when they bring good, seriousness when you are apologising, warmth when you are welcoming. The figures here show a man coming to apologise, hand on his chest and head lowered, to someone whose arms are still folded. A smile here would undo the words.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if facial expression during an apology made no difference to how it was received. ten Brinke and Adams found differences, though in a small sample of real apologies whose market effects have many causes, and in one experiment.

teach.h: The cost of acting all day.
teach.p:
Holding a professional face hour after hour is work. The sociologist Arlie Hochschild called it emotional labour: managing what you show, and sometimes what you feel, as part of a job. In 2003 Alicia Grandey distinguished two ways of doing it. Surface acting means changing your expression without changing your feeling: smiling while angry, looking calm while anxious, keeping a poker face while upset. Deep acting means changing the feeling itself, for example by seeing the situation differently, so that the expression follows.

In her study of service workers, surface acting was linked to stress, and colleagues rated the workers who relied on it as worse at delivering service with genuine warmth. Deep acting was linked to better ratings and was not linked to stress. Later research has repeatedly connected surface acting with emotional exhaustion, one of the dimensions of burnout described in Part II.

For a man who keeps a mask on all day, this is a warning. The effort of suppressing every reaction does not disappear; it accumulates. The chapter on the mask in Part II described how suppression raises physiological stress and makes partners in conversation uncomfortable. At work, it can also drain the energy you need for everything else.

The alternative is not to show every feeling, but to do less surface acting: to let genuine reactions show where they help, and where composure is needed, to work on the feeling itself, as the chapter on reappraisal in Part VI described, rather than only on the face. The figure here has slumped at the end of a long day. Some of that tiredness is the work. Some of it is the face.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if surface acting carried no cost compared with deep acting. Grandey and later research link surface acting to stress and exhaustion, though most of the evidence comes from service jobs and relies on self-report.

teach.p:
None of this means abandoning composure. There are moments when a still face is exactly right: in a negotiation, when an opponent makes an offer and you need time to think, as the chapter on negotiation later in this part describes; in a crisis, when panic would spread, as the chapter on high-stakes environments described; when you hold information you cannot share; or when someone tells you something shocking and needs you not to react.

The skill is choosing. Let your face show interest, appreciation, amusement and concern in ordinary collaboration, because those are the reactions that build trust and tell people where they stand. Save the poker face for the moments that need it. And when you are holding back, say so, so that the gap is not filled with guesses: “I'm keeping my reaction to myself until I've thought about this properly” is far better than a stony silence.

Ask how you come across. Many men with a strong poker face have no idea how forbidding it looks, and colleagues rarely say. A trusted colleague, or a recording of yourself in a meeting, as the chapter on video review described, will show you.

And as a reader, be fair to others' faces. Some people are naturally less expressive because of temperament, culture, neurodivergence or experience, and a still face from them may carry no message at all. The figures here stand angled toward each other in conversation. Between colleagues who can read each other's faces, a great deal is settled without a word.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if selective expressiveness produced no better outcomes than constant composure. The evidence on expressivity and trust supports it, though the right balance differs between workplaces and cultures.

poseGallery.annotation: A blank face after a presentation is read as disappointment. Let the reactions you actually have reach your face.

poseGallery.dontCaption: A still face while delivering bad news
poseGallery.annotation: A poker face during bad news or an apology reads as indifference. Fit the expression to the moment.
Authority does not need coldness. A moderate, genuine smile adds warmth without costing competence.

caseStudy:
Mark, forty-four, is finance director of a manufacturing firm. He spent his twenties on a trading floor, where a face that gave nothing away was a survival skill, and he still prides himself on it. In his annual 360-degree review, the comments are consistent: excellent judgement, but impossible to read. One says that people rehearse for days before taking a problem to him, because they cannot predict how he will react.

The point is driven home when Mark announces a round of redundancies. He delivers the news calmly and precisely, with no visible emotion, because he does not want to make a hard moment harder. Afterwards he learns that staff are furious: many describe him as cold and indifferent. In fact he had slept badly for a week.

With a coach, Mark watches a recording of himself in a budget meeting. His face barely moves for forty minutes, even when a junior analyst presents work he privately thinks is excellent. He starts small. He lets himself smile when an idea is good, and says so. When people bring him bad news, he lets concern show before he asks questions. When he needs time to think, he says, “I'm going to keep my reaction to myself until I've looked at the numbers.”

He keeps his poker face for the quarterly meetings with the bank, where it still serves him well. Six months later, his team begins bringing him problems earlier, and the analyst whose work he praised tells him it was the first time she had known what he thought of anything she had done.
observe: In your next meeting, notice whose faces you can read and whose you cannot, and how that affects what you say to them.
Notice your own face during a colleague's presentation, and whether your reactions reach it.
Notice how people respond when someone's face stays blank after they have spoken.
Notice moments when composure clearly helped, and moments when it was mistaken for coldness.

drills.name: Watch Your Face
steps: Record yourself, with permission, during a meeting or a practice conversation.
Watch with the sound off and count the moments your face visibly reacted.
Note moments where you felt something but your face showed nothing.
Ask a trusted colleague how readable you seem, and write down what they say.
Choose one kind of reaction, such as appreciation, to let show more often.

drills.name: Turn the Dial Up
steps: For one day, let a moderate, genuine smile show when you greet people and when something is good or funny.
Let concern show when someone brings you a problem, before you start solving it.
Write down one difference you noticed by the end of the day.

drills.name: Name the Hold
steps: Write a sentence you can use when you need to hold back a reaction, such as “I'm keeping my reaction until I've thought about it.”
Use it the next time you need time to think.
Notice whether it changes how the other person behaves.
Adjust the wording until it sounds like you.

drills.name: Fit the Moment
steps: List four situations you face at work: good news, bad news, an apology, a negotiation.
For each, write the expression that fits: warmth, concern, seriousness, composure.
Note which one you find hardest to show.
Practise that expression in front of a mirror or camera until it feels natural.
Use it the next time the situation arises.

quiz.q: A colleague says that a face which gives nothing away makes you seem more professional and trustworthy. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; inexpressive people are trusted most in every workplace
Expressive people tend to be trusted more; a blank face gives others no evidence
Expressiveness matters only in sales roles, not in other kinds of work
Trust depends entirely on what people say, and never on what their faces happen to show
quiz.explain: Research inspired by Boone and Buck links expressivity with cooperation and trust, and genuine smiles draw more trust than fake ones. A blank face offers no evidence to calibrate trust, so people fill the gap with guesses.

quiz.q: What did Wang and colleagues find about broad and slight smiles?
options: Broad smiles made people seem warmer but less competent than slight smiles
Broad smiles made people seem both warmer and more competent in all cases
Slight smiles made people seem colder and less competent than the broad smiles did
Smile intensity made no difference to judgments of warmth or competence
quiz.explain: Broad smiles raised warmth but lowered perceived competence, especially when stakes were high. A moderate, genuine smile avoids most of the trade-off.

quiz.q: What did ten Brinke and Adams find about executives' expressions during corporate apologies?
options: Executives with neutral faces protected their companies best of all
Expressions made no difference to how markets responded to apologies
Executives who smiled saw better results, because they seemed calm and confident
Smiling while apologising tended to go with worse outcomes than sadness
quiz.explain: Executives who smiled during apologies tended to see their share prices do worse, while those who looked sad tended to contain the damage. The expression must fit the moment.

quiz.q: According to Grandey's research, how did surface acting compare with deep acting?
options: Surface acting was linked to stress and to worse ratings of warm service
Surface acting was linked to less stress and to better ratings of warm service
Both forms of acting had identical effects on stress and service quality
Deep acting was linked to stress, while surface acting had no effect
quiz.explain: Changing only the expression was linked to stress and to colleagues rating service as less genuinely warm, while changing the feeling itself was linked to better ratings. Later research connects surface acting with exhaustion.

quiz.q: A junior colleague presents work you think is excellent. Your habit is to keep a neutral face and say nothing until later. What fits this chapter best?
options: Keep the neutral face, so that she does not become complacent
Wait until her annual review to tell her what you thought of it
Let your appreciation show, and tell her now what you thought of it
Give her a broad grin and a thumbs-up, but say nothing about the work itself
quiz.explain: A blank face after a presentation is usually read as disappointment. Letting genuine appreciation show, and saying so, gives her the information she needs and builds trust.

quiz.q: In a negotiation, the other side makes an offer far lower than you expected. What does this chapter suggest about your face?
options: Let your shock show fully, so they know the offer is unacceptable
This is a moment where composure helps; keep a calm face and take time to think
Smile broadly, so that they think you are pleased with the offer
Laugh at the offer, so that they realise how unrealistic it is
quiz.explain: Selective expressiveness keeps composure for moments that need it, and a negotiation is one of them. Saying you need time to think avoids the gap being filled with guesses.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific situation at work where your face, or lack of expression, was misread: as cold, disapproving, bored or indifferent. What were you actually feeling, and what did others see? Where did you learn to keep your face still? Then think of one setting where composure genuinely helps you. Describe one reaction you will let show more often, and one moment where you will keep your poker face and explain that you are doing so.
reflection.guidance: Many men only discover how unreadable they are through feedback or a recording, so if you can, watch yourself before you write. Be specific about the reaction you will let show and the words you will use when you hold back. The aim is not to perform emotion but to stop hiding the ones that would help.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat a blank face as neutral, when people fill the gap with the worst available interpretation: disapproval, boredom or contempt. The second is to hide genuine appreciation and concern, so that colleagues cannot tell where they stand and stop bringing you problems. The third is to swing to the opposite extreme, beaming broadly in high-stakes settings where a moderate expression would serve better. The fourth is to show the wrong expression for the moment, such as smiling while apologising or staying blank while delivering bad news. And the fifth is to surface act all day, suppressing every reaction, and pay for it in exhaustion. Show what helps, keep composure for the moments that need it, and say when you are holding back.
